object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier record in the supplier master, onboarded by procurement to enable purchasing.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master.
Oh. Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a vendor, used as the primary key.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
It's the primary key. It's been the primary key since before I got here.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The legal name of the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really

object_types.name: TaxId
object_types.definition: Tax identification number for a vendor; not unique due to duplicate/parent-entity records.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID.
We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The current status of a vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended.
Collapsed into three, yes. Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: Procurement-assigned tier reflecting how much is spent with the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: Compliance-assigned tier reflecting the risk level of the vendor, derived from the risk review.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A record of a risk assessment for a vendor; accumulated over time, with at most one being the current signed-off review.

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

Should RiskReview have explicit 'IsCurrent' and 'IsSignedOff' attributes/statuses to support this constraint precisely?

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.

ambiguities.description: Contact reference/identification scheme is not stated explicitly in the transcript -- only name, email, and phone are given as attributes. It's unclear whether Contact should be identified by ContactEmail, an internal contact ID, or the vendor+region combination itself (i.e., contact may not be an independent entity but rather an attribute set keyed by vendor+region). Clarify how Contact records are uniquely identified in the system.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number. ... A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact.

ambiguities.description: The 'preferred vendor' concept tracked informally in Mei's spreadsheet was explicitly excluded from modeling as it is ad hoc and has no defined rule. Confirm this remains out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called "preferred."... It's ad hoc. Don't model it.

ambiguities.description: The fourth vendor status ('run-off' or similar) for handling in-flight purchase orders after suspension is explicitly unresolved and pending a policy decision by the steering group/Legal. The model currently only supports draft/active/suspended and does not capture any post-suspension fulfillment behavior.

source_references.excerpt: Then we need a middle state. Something like run-off... This goes to the sourcing steering group. It's a policy call, not a modeling call, and Legal has to be in the room.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID is explicitly not usable as an identifier due to duplicate vendors and shared parent-entity tax IDs, but no alternative composite or grouping construct (e.g., a 'parent entity' or 'legal entity group') was defined. Is there a need to model parent/subsidiary relationships or a separate 'legal entity' concept to resolve the duplicate/aggregate-exposure problem Raj mentions?

source_references.excerpt: We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.
If we've got the same entity twice we can't see aggregate exposure.

ambiguities.description: Vendor has three addresses (remit-to, ship-from, legal) mentioned as 'frequently different and frequently wrong' but no structure, identification, or fact types were defined for these addresses since the facilitator moved on. Should Address be modeled as a value type or entity type with three distinct roles/fact types per vendor?

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: SpendTier and RiskTier are both colloquially called 'tier' by different stakeholders causing confusion; while modeled as separate fields (confirmed by Mei), it's worth flagging that naming convention enforcement ('spend tier' vs 'risk tier') has failed organizationally for two years, which may cause future requirements confusion despite the clean data model.

source_references.excerpt: And you both call it "tier." ... We both call it tier and it causes genuine chaos.
